term: "Jacobian"

## Simple explanation

A Jacobian is a table of derivatives for a function with multiple inputs and
multiple outputs. Each entry tells how much one output changes when one input
changes. It is the multivariable counterpart of a derivative and captures local
scaling, rotation, and distortion caused by a transformation.

## Technical explanation

For a differentiable function
$\mathbf{f}:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^m$ with outputs
$\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})$, its Jacobian is the $m \times n$ matrix
of first-order partial derivatives:

$$
J_{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x}) =
\begin{pmatrix}
\frac{\partial y_1}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \frac{\partial y_1}{\partial x_n} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\frac{\partial y_m}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \frac{\partial y_m}{\partial x_n}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For a small input change $\Delta \mathbf{x}$, the corresponding output change
is approximately $J_{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x})\Delta \mathbf{x}$. If $m=n$,
the determinant of the Jacobian describes the local signed change in volume;
its absolute value is used when transforming probability densities.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Automatic differentiation uses Jacobian-vector or vector-Jacobian products to
propagate gradients through vector-valued operations during neural-network
training. Normalizing flows use the log absolute determinant of a Jacobian to
correct probability densities after an invertible transformation. Jacobians
also help analyze model sensitivity and gradient behavior.

## How it works

For a vector transformation $\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})$, the chain
rule composes Jacobians. With row-vector gradients, if a loss $\mathcal{L}$
depends on $\mathbf{y}$, then

$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}
=
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{y}}
J_{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x}).
$$

For an invertible transformation $\mathbf{y}=g(\mathbf{x})$ between spaces
of equal dimension, the change-of-variables formula is

$$
p_Y(\mathbf{y}) =
p_X(g^{-1}(\mathbf{y}))
\left|\det J_{g^{-1}}(\mathbf{y})\right|.
$$

In practice, frameworks often compute Jacobian products rather than materialize
the full matrix, since a full Jacobian can be prohibitively large.

## Practical example

Consider $\mathbf{f}(x_1,x_2)=(x_1^2+x_2,\;x_1x_2)$. Its Jacobian is

$$
J_{\mathbf{f}}(x_1,x_2)=
\begin{pmatrix}
2x_1 & 1 \\
x_2 & x_1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

At a particular input, multiplying this matrix by a small input perturbation
estimates how both outputs change. Automatic-differentiation tools can compute
the same derivatives and their products for much larger models.

## Common misconceptions

- A Jacobian is a matrix of partial derivatives, not a single scalar
  derivative or the same thing as a gradient.
- A determinant is defined for a square matrix, so the usual volume-change
  interpretation requires equal input and output dimensions.
- Deep-learning libraries often avoid constructing the entire Jacobian; they
  compute only the products needed for a gradient calculation.
